blocks.title: Associated primes and localisation
blocks.body:
Let $S \subseteq A$ be multiplicative and $M$ an $A$-module.

1. If $\mathfrak p \in \operatorname{Ass} M$ and $\mathfrak p \cap S = \varnothing$, then $S^{-1}\mathfrak p \in \operatorname{Ass}_{S^{-1}A}(S^{-1}M)$.
2. If $A$ is Noetherian, every associated prime of $S^{-1}M$ arises in this way:
$$\operatorname{Ass}_{S^{-1}A}(S^{-1}M) = \{S^{-1}\mathfrak p : \mathfrak p \in \operatorname{Ass} M,\ \mathfrak p \cap S = \varnothing\}.$$
This is Guan-Hu Lemma 2.1 and Stacks Lemma 10.63.16.
3. If $A$ is Noetherian and $M$ is finitely generated, every prime minimal over $\operatorname{Ann} M$ is associated to $M$ (Guan-Hu Lemma 2.2; Stacks Lemma 10.63.8 for minimal primes of the support).

In particular, taking $S = A \setminus \mathfrak p$ in part 1: if $\mathfrak p \in \operatorname{Ass} M$ then the maximal ideal $\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}$ is associated to $M_{\mathfrak p}$, which is the step used in Guan-Hu Proposition 3.2.

1. Let $\mathfrak p = \operatorname{Ann}(x)$. We show $\operatorname{Ann}_{S^{-1}A}(x/1) = S^{-1}\mathfrak p$. If $a \in \mathfrak p$ then $(a/s)(x/1) = ax/s = 0$. Conversely, if $(a/s)(x/1) = 0$, then $uax = 0$ for some $u \in S$, so $ua \in \mathfrak p$; since $u \notin \mathfrak p$ and $\mathfrak p$ is prime, $a \in \mathfrak p$ and $a/s \in S^{-1}\mathfrak p$. The ideal $S^{-1}\mathfrak p$ is prime by the correspondence theorem (in particular proper, so $x/1 \ne 0$).

2. Let $Q = \operatorname{Ann}(x/s)$ be a prime of $S^{-1}A$ and $\mathfrak p = Q \cap A$ its contraction, a prime disjoint from $S$ with $Q = S^{-1}\mathfrak p$. As $A$ is Noetherian, $\mathfrak p = (a_1, \dots, a_n)$. Each $(a_i/1)(x/s) = 0$, so $u_ia_ix = 0$ for some $u_i \in S$. Put $u = u_1\cdots u_n$ and $y = ux$. Then $a_iy = 0$ for all $i$, so $\mathfrak p \subseteq \operatorname{Ann}(y)$. Conversely, if $by = 0$ then $(b/1)(x/s) = bx/s = bux/(us) = by/(us) = 0$, so $b/1 \in Q$ and $b \in \mathfrak p$. Thus $\mathfrak p = \operatorname{Ann}(y) \in \operatorname{Ass} M$, and $Q = S^{-1}\mathfrak p$. Together with part 1 this gives the equality.

3. Let $\mathfrak p$ be minimal over $\operatorname{Ann} M$. By the support theorem, $\mathfrak p \in V(\operatorname{Ann} M) = \operatorname{Supp} M$, so $M_{\mathfrak p} \ne 0$. The ring $A_{\mathfrak p}$ is Noetherian, so by the existence theorem $M_{\mathfrak p}$ has an associated prime, and by part 2 it is $\mathfrak qA_{\mathfrak p}$ for some $\mathfrak q \in \operatorname{Ass} M$ with $\mathfrak q \subseteq \mathfrak p$. Being the annihilator of an element of $M$, $\mathfrak q$ contains $\operatorname{Ann} M$; by minimality of $\mathfrak p$, $\mathfrak q = \mathfrak p$. This is Guan and Hu's argument: localise at the minimal prime and use that the localisation has only one prime containing the annihilator.

blocks.title: Associated primes of Z/12 and its localisations
blocks.body: Let $M = \mathbb Z/12$ as a $\mathbb Z$-module. Find $\operatorname{Ass} M$, then $\operatorname{Ass}$ of $M_{(2)}$, of $M_{(5)}$ and of $M[1/2] = S^{-1}M$ for $S = \{2^n\}$, and compare with part 3 of the theorem.
blocks.solution:
The annihilator of the class of $x \ne 0$ is $(12/\gcd(x, 12))\mathbb Z$, so the annihilators of nonzero elements are $12\mathbb Z, 6\mathbb Z, 4\mathbb Z, 3\mathbb Z, 2\mathbb Z$ (for $\gcd = 1, 2, 3, 4, 6$). The prime ones are $2\mathbb Z = \operatorname{Ann}(6)$ and $3\mathbb Z = \operatorname{Ann}(4) = \operatorname{Ann}(8)$. So $\operatorname{Ass} M = \{(2), (3)\}$. Also $\operatorname{Ann} M = 12\mathbb Z$, whose minimal primes $(2)$ and $(3)$ are both associated, as part 3 predicts; the maximal annihilators $2\mathbb Z, 3\mathbb Z$ are the primes of the existence theorem.

At $(2)$: of the two associated primes only $(2)$ is disjoint from $\mathbb Z \setminus (2)$, so $\operatorname{Ass} M_{(2)} = \{2\mathbb Z_{(2)}\}$. This matches the direct computation $M_{(2)} \cong \mathbb Z/4$ (the $3$-part dies because $3$ is inverted), where $\operatorname{Ann}(2) = 2\mathbb Z_{(2)}$.

At $(5)$: neither associated prime is contained in $(5)$, so $\operatorname{Ass} M_{(5)} = \varnothing$; indeed $M_{(5)} = 0$ because $12$ is a unit of $\mathbb Z_{(5)}$ that kills $M$, consistent with the existence theorem.

For $S = \{2^n\}$: $(2)$ meets $S$ and $(3)$ does not, so $\operatorname{Ass} S^{-1}M = \{3\mathbb Z[1/2]\}$, and indeed $S^{-1}M \cong \mathbb Z/3$ (the $\mathbb Z/4$ part is killed by $4 \in S$).

blocks.title: Regular sequences under localisation
blocks.body:
Following Stacks Definition 10.68.1, $x_1, \dots, x_r \in A$ is an $M$-regular sequence if each $x_i$ is a non-zero-divisor on $M/(x_1, \dots, x_{i-1})M$ and $M/(x_1, \dots, x_r)M \ne 0$. Let $x_1, \dots, x_r$ be $M$-regular and $S \subseteq A$ multiplicative.

1. Each $x_i/1$ is a non-zero-divisor on $S^{-1}M/(x_1/1, \dots, x_{i-1}/1)S^{-1}M$. Hence $x_1/1, \dots, x_r/1$ is $S^{-1}M$-regular as soon as $S^{-1}M/(x_1, \dots, x_r)S^{-1}M \ne 0$.
2. If $M$ is finitely generated, $\mathfrak p \in \operatorname{Supp} M$ and all $x_i \in \mathfrak p$, then $x_1/1, \dots, x_r/1$ is an $M_{\mathfrak p}$-regular sequence in $A_{\mathfrak p}$.

Part 2 is the step behind Guan-Hu Proposition 4.6, $\operatorname{depth}_{\mathfrak p} M \le \operatorname{depth} M_{\mathfrak p}$; the Stacks Project chooses this definition, without requiring the $x_i$ to lie in a maximal ideal, because it is then preserved under localisation, whereas that requirement is not preserved in passing from $A$ to $A_{\mathfrak p}$.

Write $I_i = (x_1, \dots, x_i)$. For any ideal $I$ we have $S^{-1}(IM) = (S^{-1}I)(S^{-1}M)$: an element $(\sum_j a_jm_j)/s$ with $a_j \in I$ equals $\sum_j (a_j/1)(m_j/s)$, and conversely $(a/t)(m/s) = am/(ts)$. Since localisation is exact, $S^{-1}(M/I_{i-1}M) \cong S^{-1}M/(S^{-1}I_{i-1})S^{-1}M$, and $S^{-1}I_{i-1}$ is generated by $x_1/1, \dots, x_{i-1}/1$.

1. Multiplication by $x_i$ is injective on $N = M/I_{i-1}M$, i.e. $0 \to N \xrightarrow{x_i} N$ is exact. Localising preserves exactness, and $S^{-1}$ of multiplication by $x_i$ is multiplication by $x_i/1$; so $x_i/1$ is injective on $S^{-1}N$, which is the module in the statement by the first paragraph.

2. By part 1 only the last condition needs proof. $M_{\mathfrak p}$ is a finitely generated module over the local ring $A_{\mathfrak p}$, and it is nonzero because $\mathfrak p \in \operatorname{Supp} M$. Since all $x_i/1$ lie in $\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}$, we have $(x_1, \dots, x_r)M_{\mathfrak p} \subseteq \mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}M_{\mathfrak p}$, and Nakayama's lemma gives $\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}M_{\mathfrak p} \ne M_{\mathfrak p}$. Hence $M_{\mathfrak p}/(x_1, \dots, x_r)M_{\mathfrak p} \ne 0$.

The hypothesis $x_i \in \mathfrak p$ cannot be dropped: $2$ is a $\mathbb Z$-regular sequence, but in $\mathbb Z_{(3)}$ it is a unit and $\mathbb Z_{(3)}/2\mathbb Z_{(3)} = 0$.

blocks.title: A sequence that becomes regular after localising
blocks.body: In $A = k[x, y, z]$ ($k$ a field) the Stacks Project (Example 10.68.2) notes that $x, y(1-x), z(1-x)$ is $A$-regular while $y(1-x), z(1-x), x$ is not. Verify the second claim, and show that $y(1-x), z(1-x), x$ is regular in $A_{\mathfrak m}$ for $\mathfrak m = (x, y, z)$.
blocks.solution:
In $A/(y(1-x))$ the class of $y$ is nonzero: $y = y(1-x)g$ would force $(1-x)g = 1$, impossible by degrees. But $z(1-x)\cdot y = z\cdot y(1-x) \in (y(1-x))$. So $z(1-x)$ is a zero-divisor on $A/(y(1-x))$ and the sequence is not regular.

In $A_{\mathfrak m}$ the element $1 - x \notin \mathfrak m$ is a unit. Hence $(y(1-x)) = (y)$ and $(y(1-x), z(1-x)) = (y, z)$ as ideals of $A_{\mathfrak m}$, and multiplying an element by a unit does not change whether it is a non-zero-divisor on a module. So $y(1-x), z(1-x), x$ is $A_{\mathfrak m}$-regular if and only if $y, z, x$ is. Now $y, z, x$ is $A$-regular: $A/(y) \cong k[x, z]$, on which $z$ is a non-zero-divisor; $A/(y, z) \cong k[x]$, on which $x$ is a non-zero-divisor; and $A/(y, z, x) \cong k \ne 0$. All three lie in $\mathfrak m$, $A$ is finitely generated over itself and $\mathfrak m \in \operatorname{Supp} A$, so part 2 of the theorem shows that $y, z, x$ is $A_{\mathfrak m}$-regular. (Stacks Lemma 10.68.4 explains the general phenomenon: over a Noetherian local ring every permutation of a regular sequence of a finitely generated module is regular.)

blocks.title: Localisation is flat but rarely faithfully flat

blocks.body:
$S^{-1}A$ is flat over $A$ because localisation is exact and $S^{-1}N \cong N \otimes_A S^{-1}A$. So (1) and (2) are equivalent by Stacks Lemma 10.39.16.

(2) implies (4): the image of $\operatorname{Spec} S^{-1}A$ is the set of primes disjoint from $S$. If some $s \in S$ were not a unit, it would lie in a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$, which meets $S$ and so is not in the image.

(3) implies (4): if $s \in S$ is not a unit, then $N = A/sA \ne 0$, but $S^{-1}N = 0$, because for $n \in N$ and $t \in S$ we have $n/t = sn/(st) = 0$, as $sn = 0$ in $N$.

(4) implies (1), (2), (3): if $S$ consists of units then $\iota\colon A \to S^{-1}A$ satisfies Strickland's conditions with $B = A$ and the identity map (every $a/s$ equals $\iota(as^{-1})$, and $sa = 0$ forces $a = 0$), so $\iota$ is an isomorphism, and an isomorphism has all three properties.

For the last sentence, $A \setminus \mathfrak p$ consists of units exactly when every non-unit lies in $\mathfrak p$, i.e. when $\mathfrak p$ is the unique maximal ideal.

- An $M$-regular sequence need not stay regular in $A_{\mathfrak p}$ if some $x_i \notin \mathfrak p$: the quotient can become zero. Conversely, a sequence can be regular in some $A_{\mathfrak m}$ without being regular in $A$ (the example above, at $\mathfrak m = (x, y, z)$). Each single condition "$x_i$ is a non-zero-divisor on $M/I_{i-1}M$" is a local property, since it says that a kernel vanishes, so the failure in $A$ must show up at some other maximal ideal: in the example, at one containing $1 - x$, where $x$ becomes a unit.
- Texts on local rings often require the elements of a regular sequence to lie in the maximal ideal; the Stacks Project does not, and it is the version without this requirement that localises.
- Flatness of $A_{\mathfrak p}$ lets one push exact sequences and regular sequences forward, but faithful flatness, which would let one pull properties back from $A_{\mathfrak p}$ to $A$, fails unless $A$ is local with maximal ideal $\mathfrak p$. Properties of $A$ are recovered from all localisations together, by the local-global principle of the next section; this is why Guan and Hu prove separate lemmas for $R \to R_{\mathfrak p}$ rather than apply general faithfully flat base change.

1. (Basic) Find $\operatorname{Ass}_{\mathbb Z}(\mathbb Z/360)$, and use the localisation theorem to find the associated primes of $(\mathbb Z/360)_{(3)}$ and of $S^{-1}(\mathbb Z/360)$ for $S = \{5^n\}$.
2. (Basic) Let $A$ be Noetherian and $M \ne 0$. Show that the set of zero-divisors on $M$ is exactly the union of the associated primes of $M$.
3. (Medium) Let $A = k[x, y]$ and $M = A/(x^2, xy)$. Show that $\operatorname{Ass} M = \{(x), (x, y)\}$ (find elements with these annihilators and show there are no others), and compute $\operatorname{Ass} M_{(x)}$ and $\operatorname{Ass} M_{(x,y)}$.
4. (Medium) Let $A$ be Noetherian and $M$ any $A$-module. Show that $\mathfrak p \in \operatorname{Supp} M$ if and only if some associated prime of $M$ is contained in $\mathfrak p$.
5. (Harder) Show that $x \in A$ is a non-zero-divisor on $M$ if and only if $x/1$ is a non-zero-divisor on $M_{\mathfrak m}$ for every maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$, and deduce that for $M$ finitely generated over a Noetherian ring, a sequence $x_1, \dots, x_r$ with $M/(x_1, \dots, x_r)M \ne 0$ is $M$-regular if and only if, for every maximal $\mathfrak m$, its image satisfies the non-zero-divisor conditions on $M_{\mathfrak m}$.

blocks.title: Local properties and the local-global principle
blocks.body: A property of rings or modules is local if it holds for $A$ (or $M$) exactly when it holds for every localisation $A_{\mathfrak p}$ (or $M_{\mathfrak p}$), equivalently for every $A_{\mathfrak m}$ with $\mathfrak m$ maximal. Atiyah-Macdonald have a section called Local properties, Gathmann proves the basic cases in Proposition 6.27 and the exercises after it, and Lombardi gives "concrete" versions in which the infinitely many primes are replaced by finitely many elements generating the unit ideal. The second form is the one that glues: it is the algebra behind the structure sheaf of an affine scheme.

blocks.title: Basic local properties
blocks.body:
Let $M$ be an $A$-module. The following hold, and in each case "for all primes" may be replaced by "for all maximal ideals".

1. $M = 0$ if and only if $M_{\mathfrak p} = 0$ for all primes $\mathfrak p$.
2. A sequence $L \to M \to N$ is exact if and only if all $L_{\mathfrak p} \to M_{\mathfrak p} \to N_{\mathfrak p}$ are exact. In particular injectivity and surjectivity of a map are local.
3. For submodules $N, N' \subseteq M$: $N \subseteq N'$ iff $N_{\mathfrak p} \subseteq N'_{\mathfrak p}$ for all $\mathfrak p$; so equality of ideals is local.
4. $A$ is reduced iff every $A_{\mathfrak p}$ is reduced.
5. An element $x \in M$ is zero iff $x/1 = 0$ in every $M_{\mathfrak m}$.

5 (and hence 1). Suppose $x \ne 0$. Its annihilator $\operatorname{Ann}(x)$ is a proper ideal (it misses $1$), so it is contained in some maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$. If $x/1 = 0$ in $M_{\mathfrak m}$ there is $s \notin \mathfrak m$ with $sx = 0$, i.e. $s \in \operatorname{Ann}(x) \subseteq \mathfrak m$, a contradiction. So some $x/1 \ne 0$. Applying this to every $x$ gives 1 for maximal ideals; the version with all primes follows since $M_{\mathfrak m} = 0$ is among the conditions.

2. One direction is exactness of localisation. Conversely let $H = \ker(M \to N)/\operatorname{im}(L \to M)$. Localisation commutes with kernels, images and quotients, so $H_{\mathfrak m}$ is the homology of the localised sequence, which is $0$. By 1, $H = 0$.

3. Apply 1 to $(N + N')/N'$, whose localisation is $(N_{\mathfrak p} + N'_{\mathfrak p})/N'_{\mathfrak p}$.

4. The nilradical commutes with localisation (exercise 4 of the section on ideals, or part 6 of the extension theorem applied to $I = 0$): $\sqrt{0}_{\mathfrak p} = \sqrt{0_{A_{\mathfrak p}}}$. By 1, $\sqrt 0 = 0$ iff all its localisations vanish.

blocks.title: Being a domain is not local
blocks.body: Let $A = \mathbb Z/6$. Show that every localisation of $A$ at a prime is a field, but $A$ is not a domain.
blocks.solution: $A \cong \mathbb Z/2 \times \mathbb Z/3$ has the two primes $\mathfrak p_2 = (2)$ and $\mathfrak p_3 = (3)$. At $\mathfrak p_2$, the element $3 \notin \mathfrak p_2$ becomes invertible, and $3 \cdot 2 = 0$, so $2/1 = 0$; hence $A_{\mathfrak p_2}$ is a quotient of $A/(2) = \mathbb F_2$, and it is nonzero (localising at a prime never gives $0$), so $A_{\mathfrak p_2} \cong \mathbb F_2$. Similarly $A_{\mathfrak p_3} \cong \mathbb F_3$. Both are fields, in particular domains, but $2 \cdot 3 = 0$ in $A$. Gathmann's Exercise 6.29 asks for exactly this phenomenon (being a domain is not a local property), and Wikipedia mentions a more drastic case: an infinite product of fields is neither a domain nor Noetherian, although all its local rings are fields. Geometrically, $\operatorname{Spec} A$ is two points, and a domain must have irreducible spectrum, a condition that cannot be seen one point at a time.

blocks.title: Concrete local-global principle

blocks.body:
First, for any $N \ge 1$ the powers $s_1^N, \dots, s_n^N$ also generate the unit ideal: from $1 = \sum c_is_i$, raising to the power $n(N-1) + 1$ and expanding, every monomial contains some $s_i$ with exponent at least $N$.

1. $m/1 = 0$ in $M_{s_i}$ means $s_i^{N_i}m = 0$. Take $N = \max N_i$ and write $1 = \sum d_is_i^N$; then $m = \sum d_is_i^Nm = 0$.

2. If $a/1$ is a unit in $A_{s_i}$ then $(a/1)(b_i/s_i^{k}) = 1$, so $s_i^{l}(ab_i - s_i^{k}) = 0$ and $s_i^{k+l} \in aA$. So the ideal $aA$ contains a power of each $s_i$, hence a set of elements generating the unit ideal (raise to a common exponent as above), so $aA = A$.

3. If $ab = 0$ then $(a/1)(b/1) = 0$ in each $A_{s_i}$, so $b/1 = 0$ in each $A_{s_i}$, and $b = 0$ by 1. The converse uses that $A \to A_{s_i}$ is flat: multiplication by $a$ is injective on $A$, hence on $A_{s_i}$ by exactness.

blocks.title: Glueing: the sheaf condition for localisations
blocks.body:
Let $f_1, \dots, f_n$ generate the unit ideal of $A$ and let $M$ be an $A$-module. Then the sequence
$$0 \to M \xrightarrow{\ \alpha\ } \bigoplus_{i} M_{f_i} \xrightarrow{\ \beta\ } \bigoplus_{i,j} M_{f_if_j}$$
is exact, where $\alpha(m) = (m/1)_i$ and $\beta\big((m_i)_i\big) = (m_i - m_j)_{i,j}$, the differences being taken in $M_{f_if_j}$ (into which both $M_{f_i}$ and $M_{f_j}$ map).

This is the Stacks Project's argument (Lemma 10.24.1). By the local properties above, exactness may be checked after localising at each maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$. Localising at $\mathfrak m$ commutes with the finite direct sums and with the localisations $M_{f_i}$ (localisation in stages: both $(M_{f_i})_{\mathfrak m}$ and $(M_{\mathfrak m})_{f_i}$ invert the same multiplicative set). Since the $f_i$ generate the unit ideal, not all lie in $\mathfrak m$; renumber so that $f_1 \notin \mathfrak m$. After localising, $f_1$ is a unit, and we may assume $f_1 = 1$, so $M_{f_1} = M$ and $M_{f_1f_j} = M_{f_j}$.

Now $\alpha$ is injective, because its first component is the identity of $M$. If $(m_i) \in \ker\beta$, then in particular $m_1 - m_j = 0$ in $M_{f_1f_j} = M_{f_j}$ for every $j$, i.e. $m_j$ is the image of $m_1 \in M$. Thus $(m_i) = \alpha(m_1)$.

blocks.caption: The glueing sequence for $A = M = \mathbb Z$ and the generators $f_1 = 2$, $f_2 = 3$ of the unit ideal (keeping only the component $(1,2)$ of $\beta$, as the others are $0$ or determined by it), with $\beta(x, y) = x - y$. Exactness in the middle says $\mathbb Z[1/2] \cap \mathbb Z[1/3] = \mathbb Z$ inside $\mathbb Z[1/6]$: a rational number whose denominator is both a power of $2$ and a power of $3$ is an integer.
blocks.alt: An exact sequence: 0, then Z, then the direct sum of Z[1/2] and Z[1/3], then Z[1/6], with arrows alpha and beta.

items.label: Algebraic
items.body: A property is local when it can be tested on all $A_{\mathfrak p}$, or all $A_{\mathfrak m}$; the proofs reduce to the fact that a module whose localisations vanish is zero.

items.label: Geometric
items.body: Localising at $f$ restricts to the open set $D(f)$, where $f$ does not vanish; localising at $\mathfrak p$ keeps only the germs of functions at the point $\mathfrak p$. The nLab phrases this through the duality between rings and spaces: $\operatorname{Spec} R[S^{-1}] \to \operatorname{Spec} R$ are the basic open immersions.

items.label: Constructive
items.body: Lombardi replaces "for every prime" by "on each $A[1/s_i]$ for finitely many comaximal $s_i$". The abstract principle (all primes) needs choice to produce primes; the concrete one does not, and Lombardi shows how proofs using the abstract version can be turned into algorithms that output the $s_i$.

items.label: Not very local
items.body: Grossack points out that Zariski open sets are dense, so the local ring $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ still remembers a lot of global information: for varieties over an algebraically closed field $k$, if the local rings at a point of $X$ and a point of $Y$ are isomorphic as $k$-algebras, the points have isomorphic open neighbourhoods, so $X$ and $Y$ are birational. To see a genuinely small neighbourhood one completes: by the Cohen structure theorem, regular points of varieties of the same dimension over $k$ all have completed local ring $k[\![x_1, \dots, x_n]\!]$, as in the manifold picture.

blocks.title: Global notions defined locally
blocks.body:
Many classes of rings are defined by a condition on all localisations, and a theorem then shows that maximal ideals suffice.

1. Regular rings: $A$ is regular if every $A_{\mathfrak p}$ is a regular local ring (Guan-Hu Definition 5.18); it suffices to check maximal ideals (their Theorem 5.20).
2. Cohen-Macaulay rings: every $A_{\mathfrak p}$ is a Cohen-Macaulay local ring (Definition 4.11); again maximal ideals suffice (Lemma 4.12).
3. Dedekind domains: a Noetherian domain all of whose localisations at nonzero primes are discrete valuation rings (Sutherland, Proposition 2.9 and Definition 2.10; see the next section).
4. Homological invariants: for a finitely generated module over a Noetherian ring, $\operatorname{pd} M = \sup_{\mathfrak p} \operatorname{pd} M_{\mathfrak p}$ and $\operatorname{gldim} A = \sup_{\mathfrak p} \operatorname{gldim} A_{\mathfrak p}$ (Guan-Hu Lemmas 2.9 and 2.14); localisation can only lower projective dimension (Lemma 2.10), because it carries projective resolutions to projective resolutions.
5. Projective modules: a finitely presented module is projective iff all its localisations are free; concretely (Lombardi) iff there are comaximal $s_i$ with each $M_{s_i}$ free.

The definitions of regular and Cohen-Macaulay local rings are not given here; see [[homological-algebra]] for the tools, and Guan-Hu for a complete formal treatment.

blocks.title: Localising at an idempotent
blocks.body: If $e \in A$ is idempotent ($e^2 = e$), then $A_e \cong A/(1 - e) \cong eA$, where $eA$ is a ring with identity $e$. If $e_1, \dots, e_n$ are orthogonal idempotents with $\sum e_i = 1$, then $A \cong A_{e_1} \times \dots \times A_{e_n}$, and similarly for modules.

The map $A \to A/(1-e)$ sends $e$ to $1$, a unit, so it factors through $A_e$; and in $A_e$ we have $e/1 \cdot (1 - e)/1 = 0$ with $e/1$ a unit, so $1 - e$ dies, giving the inverse map $A/(1-e) \to A_e$. The map $A \to eA$, $a \mapsto ea$, is a surjective ring map with kernel $(1 - e)A$ (if $ea = 0$ then $a = (1-e)a$). For orthogonal idempotents, $A \to \prod eA$, $a \mapsto (e_ia)_i$, is an isomorphism with inverse $(a_i) \mapsto \sum a_i$, which is Lombardi's Fait 1.17.

blocks.title: Glueing and idempotents in a small ring
blocks.body: (a) In $A = \mathbb Z/6$ find the idempotents and compute $A_e$ for each. (b) For the glueing sequence with $A = \mathbb Z$, $f_1 = 2$, $f_2 = 3$, take $x = 5/2 \in \mathbb Z[1/2]$ and $y = 7/3 \in \mathbb Z[1/3]$. Compute $\beta(x, y)$, decide whether $(x, y)$ lies in the image of $\alpha$, and describe all pairs in $\ker\beta$.
blocks.solution:
(a) $e^2 = e$ in $\mathbb Z/6$ means $6 \mid e(e-1)$: $e \in \{0, 1, 3, 4\}$. Then $A_0 = 0$, $A_1 = A$, $A_3 \cong A/(1 - 3) = A/(2) \cong \mathbb F_2$ and $A_4 \cong A/(1-4) = A/(3) \cong \mathbb F_3$. The orthogonal pair $3, 4$ (indeed $3\cdot 4 = 12 \equiv 0$ and $3 + 4 \equiv 1$) recovers $\mathbb Z/6 \cong \mathbb F_2 \times \mathbb F_3$. Inverting the idempotent $3$ gives the same ring as localising at the prime $(2)$, computed in the example on domains.

(b) $\beta(x, y) = 5/2 - 7/3 = 1/6 \ne 0$ in $\mathbb Z[1/6]$, so $(x, y) \notin \ker\beta = \operatorname{im}\alpha$. In general a pair $(x, y)$ with $x = y$ in $\mathbb Z[1/6]$ must have $x \in \mathbb Z[1/2] \cap \mathbb Z[1/3] = \mathbb Z$, and then $(x, y) = \alpha(x)$. The partition of unity behind the proof is $1 = (-1)\cdot 2 + 1 \cdot 3$.

blocks.body:
1. (Basic) Show that an $A$-module map $\varphi\colon M \to N$ is an isomorphism iff every $\varphi_{\mathfrak m}$ is.
2. (Basic) Find comaximal $s_1, s_2 \in \mathbb Z$ such that $\mathbb Z[1/s_1]$ and $\mathbb Z[1/s_2]$ are both PIDs with $\mathbb Z = \mathbb Z[1/s_1] \cap \mathbb Z[1/s_2]$, and check the glueing sequence by hand.
3. (Medium) Show that $\operatorname{Spec} A$ is covered by finitely many $D(f_i)$ iff the $f_i$ generate the unit ideal, and deduce that $\operatorname{Spec} A$ is quasi-compact.
4. (Medium) Show that being Noetherian is not a local property, using an infinite product of fields $\prod_{\mathbb N} \mathbb F_2$: every localisation at a prime is a field. (You may use that every element $x$ of this ring is idempotent.)
5. (Harder) Prove the glueing theorem directly, without localising at maximal ideals: given elements $m_i/f_i^N \in M_{f_i}$ that agree in every $M_{f_if_j}$, use an equation $1 = \sum_i c_if_i^K$ for a suitable $K$ to write down $m \in M$ with $m/1 = m_i/f_i^N$ in each $M_{f_i}$.

blocks.title: Affine schemes in one paragraph
blocks.body:
The two theorems above are why localisations are the local functions of algebraic geometry. On $X = \operatorname{Spec} A$ the open sets $D(f)$ form a basis, $D(f) \cap D(g) = D(fg)$, and $D(f) \subseteq D(g)$ gives a restriction map $A_g \to A_f$ (since $g$ is then invertible in $A_f$). Assigning $A_f$ to $D(f)$ defines a sheaf on this basis, because if $D(f) = \bigcup_i D(f_i)$ then the $f_i$ generate the unit ideal of $A_f$ and the glueing sequence for the ring $A_f$ is exactly the sheaf condition. The resulting sheaf $\mathcal O_X$ satisfies (Stacks Lemma 26.5.4; Vakil §5.1)
$$\Gamma(X, \mathcal O_X) = A,\qquad \Gamma(D(f), \mathcal O_X) = A_f,\qquad \mathcal O_{X, \mathfrak p} = A_{\mathfrak p},$$
the last because the stalk is the colimit of the $A_f$ over $f \notin \mathfrak p$, which is $A_{\mathfrak p}$ by the colimit description of localisation. Its stalks are local rings, so $(X, \mathcal O_X)$ is a locally ringed space, and a ring map $A \to B$ induces a morphism of locally ringed spaces $\operatorname{Spec} B \to \operatorname{Spec} A$ (the stalk maps $A_{\mathfrak q^c} \to B_{\mathfrak q}$ are local). Xu's paper reproduces these steps for commutative $\mathbb F_1$-algebras: the universal property of $S^{-1}A$ (his Theorem 3.5), then stalks $A_{\mathfrak p}$, sections $A_f$ over $D(f)$ and global sections $A$ (Theorem 5.4), with morphisms required to be local on stalks (Definition 5.5), and obtains an anti-equivalence between commutative $\mathbb F_1$-algebras and what he calls absolute affine schemes. The details belong to [[schemes]].

1. (Basic) Show that if $D(f) \subseteq D(g)$ then $g$ is a unit in $A_f$, so there is a unique map $A_g \to A_f$ under $A$.
2. (Basic) For $X = \operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z$ compute the stalks at $(0)$ and at $(p)$, and $\Gamma(D(6), \mathcal O_X)$.
3. (Medium) Show that if $D(f) = D(g)$ then $A_f$ and $A_g$ are canonically isomorphic under $A$, although they need not be equal as sets of fractions.
4. (Medium) Let $\varphi\colon A \to B$ be a ring map, $\mathfrak q$ a prime of $B$ and $\mathfrak p = \varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak q)$. Show that the induced map $A_{\mathfrak p} \to B_{\mathfrak q}$ is a local homomorphism.

blocks.title: Arithmetic: discrete valuation rings and Dedekind domains
blocks.body: In number theory localisation is used to make ideal theory simple. The ring of integers $\mathcal O_K$ of a number field may lack unique factorisation (see [[ideals]]), but each localisation $\mathcal O_{K,\mathfrak p}$ at a nonzero prime is a discrete valuation ring, a ring whose ideals are just the powers of one prime element. Global information is recovered because a domain is the intersection of its localisations. Sutherland's lecture develops exactly this, and Coykendall and Kettinger study class groups of the rings $\mathcal O_K[1/\alpha]$ obtained by inverting one element.

blocks.title: Discrete valuation ring
blocks.body: A discrete valuation on a field $K$ is a surjective map $v\colon K^\times \to \mathbb Z$ with $v(xy) = v(x) + v(y)$ and $v(x + y) \ge \min(v(x), v(y))$ (when $x + y \ne 0$). Its valuation ring $R = \{x \in K^\times : v(x) \ge 0\} \cup \{0\}$ is a discrete valuation ring (DVR). An element $\pi$ with $v(\pi) = 1$ is a uniformiser. A DVR is a local principal ideal domain: its units are the elements of valuation $0$, its maximal ideal is $\pi R$, and every nonzero ideal is $\pi^kR$ for a unique $k \ge 0$. For a Noetherian local domain of dimension one, being a DVR is equivalent to being integrally closed, and also to the maximal ideal being principal (Stacks Lemma 10.119.7, which lists further equivalent conditions).

blocks.title: Localising the integers at a prime
blocks.body: Show that $\mathbb Z_{(p)}$ is the valuation ring of the $p$-adic valuation $v_p$ on $\mathbb Q$, find its units and ideals, and its residue field. Do the same for $k[x]_{(x-2)}$.
blocks.solution:
Write a nonzero rational as $x = p^k a/b$ with $p 
mid ab$; then $v_p(x) = k$ is well defined, additive under products, and $v_p(x + y) \ge \min(v_p(x), v_p(y))$ (factor out the smaller power of $p$). $x \in \mathbb Z_{(p)}$ iff it has a representative with denominator prime to $p$ iff $k \ge 0$. Units: $v_p(x) = 0$, i.e. $x = a/b$ with $p 
mid ab$. Every nonzero $x \in \mathbb Z_{(p)}$ is $p^{v_p(x)}u$ with $u$ a unit, so an ideal $I 
e 0$ equals $p^k\mathbb Z_{(p)}$ with $k$ the least valuation in $I$; here $\pi = p$. The residue field is $\mathbb Z_{(p)}/p\mathbb Z_{(p)} \cong \operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb Z/p) = \mathbb F_p$, as in the theorem on the local ring at a prime.

For $k[x]_{(x-2)}$, the rational functions defined at $2$, the valuation is the order of vanishing at $2$, the uniformiser is $x - 2$, the maximal ideal is the set of functions vanishing at $2$, and the residue field is $k$, via evaluation at $2$ (Sutherland, Example 2.4).

blocks.title: What localisation preserves
blocks.body:
Let $A$ be a domain and $S$ multiplicative with $0 \notin S$.

1. If $A$ is Noetherian, so is $S^{-1}A$; and $\dim S^{-1}A \le \dim A$.
2. Integral closure commutes with localisation: if $A \to B$ is a ring map and $B'$ is the integral closure of $A$ in $B$, then the integral closure of $S^{-1}A$ in $S^{-1}B$ is $S^{-1}B'$. In particular, if $A$ is integrally closed, so is $S^{-1}A$.
3. If $A$ is a Dedekind domain (Noetherian, integrally closed, every nonzero prime maximal), so is $S^{-1}A$.

1. Noetherian: proved in the section on ideals. Dimension: chains of primes in $S^{-1}A$ correspond to chains of primes of $A$ avoiding $S$.

2. (Stacks Lemma 10.36.11.) Elements of $S^{-1}B'$ are integral over $S^{-1}A$: if $b$ satisfies a monic equation over $A$, then $b/s$ satisfies the equation obtained by dividing by $s^n$, monic over $S^{-1}A$. Conversely, let $b/t \in S^{-1}B$ satisfy
$$(b/t)^n + (a_1/s_1)(b/t)^{n-1} + \dots + a_n/s_n = 0 .$$
Put $s = s_1\cdots s_n$ and multiply by $(st)^n$: we get $(sb)^n + c_1(sb)^{n-1} + \dots + c_n = 0$ in $S^{-1}B$ with $c_i \in A$ (each $c_i$ is $a_i$ times a product of the $s_j$ and of powers of $t$). So some $u \in S$ kills the left side in $B$; multiplying by $u^n$ gives a monic equation for $usb$ over $A$ in $B$. Hence $usb \in B'$ and $b/t = usb/ust \in S^{-1}B'$. Sutherland gives the same clearing-of-denominators argument for $B = \operatorname{Frac}(A)$, which is the second sentence.

3. Noetherian and integrally closed by 1 and 2. A nonzero prime of $S^{-1}A$ is $\mathfrak p^e$ with $\mathfrak p \ne 0$, so $\mathfrak p$ is maximal in $A$; any prime of $S^{-1}A$ containing $\mathfrak p^e$ contracts to a prime containing $\mathfrak p$, hence to $\mathfrak p$, so $\mathfrak p^e$ is maximal.

blocks.title: A domain is the intersection of its localisations
blocks.body:
Let $A$ be a domain with fraction field $K$. Inside $K$,
$$A = \bigcap_{\mathfrak m \text{ maximal}} A_{\mathfrak m} = \bigcap_{\mathfrak p \text{ prime}} A_{\mathfrak p}.$$
For example $\mathbb Z = \bigcap_p \mathbb Z_{(p)}$.

Clearly $A$ lies in every $A_{\mathfrak p}$, and $\bigcap_{\mathfrak p} \subseteq \bigcap_{\mathfrak m}$. Let $x \in K$ lie in every $A_{\mathfrak m}$ and consider the ideal of denominators $D = \{d \in A : dx \in A\}$. For each $\mathfrak m$ write $x = a/s$ with $s \notin \mathfrak m$; then $sx = a \in A$, so $s \in D \setminus \mathfrak m$. Thus $D$ is contained in no maximal ideal, so $D = A$, $1 \in D$, and $x \in A$. (Sutherland deduces the statement, also for ideals and modules, from his Proposition 2.6.)

blocks.title: Dedekind domains are locally DVRs
blocks.body: For a Noetherian domain $A$ the following are equivalent: (i) $A_{\mathfrak p}$ is a DVR for every nonzero prime $\mathfrak p$; (ii) $A$ is integrally closed and $\dim A \le 1$. Such $A$ is a Dedekind domain. Every PID, in particular $\mathbb Z$ and $k[x]$, is a Dedekind domain.

(ii) implies (i): $A_{\mathfrak p}$ is a Noetherian local domain, integrally closed by part 2 of the preservation theorem, and of dimension $1$ (its primes are $0$ and $\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}$). By the characterisation of DVRs among Noetherian local domains of dimension one (Stacks Lemma 10.119.7; Sutherland quotes the same fact from his first lecture in the proof of his Proposition 2.9), it is a DVR.

(i) implies (ii): a DVR is integrally closed (if $x \notin R$ then $v(x) < 0$, and in a monic equation $x^n + a_1x^{n-1} + \dots + a_n = 0$ the term $x^n$ has strictly smaller valuation than all the others, which is impossible), so by the intersection theorem $A = \bigcap A_{\mathfrak p}$ is an intersection of integrally closed rings with the same fraction field, hence integrally closed. If $0 \ne \mathfrak q \subsetneq \mathfrak p$ were a chain of primes in $A$, then $A_{\mathfrak p}$ would have the chain $0 \subsetneq \mathfrak qA_{\mathfrak p} \subsetneq \mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}$, but a DVR has only two primes. For a PID, each $A_{\mathfrak p}$ is a local PID that is not a field, which is a DVR (the valuation is the exponent of a generator of $\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}$).

blocks.title: A non-principal prime becomes principal locally
blocks.body: In $D = \mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ let $P_2 = (2, 1 + \sqrt{-5})$, the prime with $P_2^2 = (2)$ from [[ideals]]. Show that $P_2D_{P_2}$ is generated by $1 + \sqrt{-5}$, so $D_{P_2}$ is a DVR with uniformiser $1 + \sqrt{-5}$, although $P_2$ is not principal in $D$.
blocks.solution:
In $D_{P_2}$ the element $3$ is a unit, since $3 \notin P_2$ (elements of $P_2$ are $a + b\sqrt{-5}$ with $a \equiv b \pmod 2$). Now $(1 + \sqrt{-5})(1 - \sqrt{-5}) = 1 + 5 = 6$, so
$$2 = \frac{(1 + \sqrt{-5})(1 - \sqrt{-5})}{3} \in (1 + \sqrt{-5})D_{P_2}.$$
Hence $P_2D_{P_2} = (2, 1 + \sqrt{-5})D_{P_2} = (1 + \sqrt{-5})D_{P_2}$. The local ring is a DVR because $D$ is a Dedekind domain. The valuation of $2$ is $2$ (as $(2) = P_2^2$) and that of $1 + \sqrt{-5}$ is $1$ (as $(1 + \sqrt{-5}) = P_2P_3$ with $P_3 = (3, 1+\sqrt{-5}) \ne P_2$). Locally at $P_2$ the failure of unique factorisation is invisible: it is a global phenomenon, measured by the class group.

blocks.title: Class groups of localisations (Claborn)
blocks.body:
Let $D$ be a Dedekind domain and $\alpha \in D$ a nonzero non-unit with $(\alpha) = \mathfrak p_1^{n_1}\cdots\mathfrak p_k^{n_k}$. Then
$$\operatorname{Cl}(D[1/\alpha]) \cong \operatorname{Cl}(D)/\langle[\mathfrak p_1], \dots, [\mathfrak p_k]\rangle .$$
This is Theorem 4.1 of Coykendall-Kettinger, a special case of a theorem of Claborn; the proof is not given here (see [coyk] §4 and the references there). Their Theorem 4.2 states that $\mathcal O_K[1/\alpha]$ is the integral closure of $\mathbb Z[1/N(\alpha)]$ in $K$; read it with care, because the integral closure is $\mathcal O_K[1/N(\alpha)]$, which contains $\mathcal O_K[1/\alpha]$ and can be strictly larger (see the example 'Inverting an element versus inverting its norm' below; equality holds for instance when $\alpha \in \mathbb Z$, the case of their Theorem 4.5). They also use (Proposition 5.2, due to Gilmer) that every ring between a Dedekind domain $D$ and its fraction field is an intersection of localisations $D_{\mathfrak p}$.

blocks.title: Inverting 2 in Z[sqrt(-5)]
blocks.body: Using the theorem, compute $\operatorname{Cl}(\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}][1/2])$, and verify by hand that the non-principal prime $P_3' = (3, 1 - \sqrt{-5})$ becomes principal in $D[1/2]$.
blocks.solution:
(This is our application of their Theorem 4.1; the paper's own examples invert other elements.) $\operatorname{Cl}(D) \cong \mathbb Z/2$, generated by the class of the non-principal prime $P_2$ (see [[class-group]]). Since $(2) = P_2^2$, the theorem gives $\operatorname{Cl}(D[1/2]) \cong \operatorname{Cl}(D)/\langle [P_2] \rangle = 0$: the ring $D[1/2]$ is a PID.

By hand: in $D$ we have $P_2P_3' = (1 - \sqrt{-5})$ (an exercise on [[ideals]], checked below). Extension is multiplicative, $(IJ)^e = I^eJ^e$, and $P_2^e = D[1/2]$ because $2 \in P_2$ is a unit of $D[1/2]$. So
$$P_3'D[1/2] = P_2^eP_3'^e = (P_2P_3')^e = (1 - \sqrt{-5})D[1/2].$$

blocks.title: A localisation is the intersection of its local rings
blocks.body:
Let $A$ be a domain with fraction field $K$ and $S$ multiplicative with $0 
otin S$. Inside $K$,
$$S^{-1}A =  igcap_{\mathfrak p \cap S = \varnothing} A_{\mathfrak p},$$
the intersection over primes of $A$ disjoint from $S$; and for a prime $\mathfrak p$ of $A$, $\mathfrak pS^{-1}A

The second statement is part 3 of the extension-contraction theorem. For the first, put $B = S^{-1}A \subseteq K$, a domain with fraction field $K$. By the theorem that a domain is the intersection of its localisations, $B =  igcap_Q B_Q$ over the primes $Q$ of $B$, and these are the $Q = S^{-1}\mathfrak p$ with $\mathfrak p \cap S = \varnothing$. It remains to see $B_Q = A_{\mathfrak p}$ as subrings of $K$. If $t \in A \setminus \mathfrak p$ then $t/1

blocks.title: Inverting an element versus inverting its norm
blocks.body: Let $K = \mathbb Q(i)$, $\mathcal O_K = \mathbb Z[i]$ and $\alpha = 2 + i$, so $N(\alpha) = 5$. Is $R = \mathbb Z[i][1/\alpha]$ the integral closure of $\mathbb Z[1/5]$ in $K$? Then describe in general, for a number field $K$ and nonzero $\alpha \in \mathcal O_K$, how $\mathcal O_K[1/\alpha]$ and $\mathcal O_K[1/N(\alpha)]$ compare.
blocks.solution:
By the theorem on what localisation preserves (part 2, with $A = \mathbb Z$, $B = K$, $B' = \mathcal O_K = \mathbb Z[i]$ and $S = \{5^n\}$, noting $S^{-1}K = K$), the integral closure of $\mathbb Z[1/5]$ in $K$ is $\mathbb Z[i][1/5]$. It contains $R$, since $1/(2+i) = (2-i)/5$. But it is strictly larger. In the PID $\mathbb Z[i]$ we have $5 = (2+i)(2-i)$, and $2 - i$ is a Gaussian prime (its norm $5$ is prime) that is not an associate of $2+i$ (the associates of $2+i$ are $\pm(2+i)$ and $\pm(1-2i)$). By unique factorisation no power $(2+i)^n$ is divisible by $2 - i$, so the prime $(2-i)$ is disjoint from $\{(2+i)^n\}$ and extends to a proper prime of $R$ containing $5$. Thus $5$ is not a unit of $R$: $1/5 \notin R$, and $R$ does not even contain $\mathbb Z[1/5]$.

In general, let $N(\alpha)$ be the product of the conjugates of $\alpha$ and $\beta = N(\alpha)/\alpha$, the product of the conjugates other than $\alpha$ itself. Then $\beta \in K$ and $\beta$ is an algebraic integer, so $\beta \in \mathcal O_K$, and $1/\alpha = \beta/N(\alpha)$. Hence always $\mathcal O_K[1/\alpha] \subseteq \mathcal O_K[1/N(\alpha)]$, the latter being the integral closure of $\mathbb Z[1/N(\alpha)]$ in $K$. Equality holds if and only if $N(\alpha)$ is a unit of $\mathcal O_K[1/\alpha]$, that is (by the description of the saturation of $\{\alpha^n\}$ as the complement of the union of the primes not containing $\alpha$) if and only if every prime of $\mathcal O_K$ containing $N(\alpha)$ contains $\alpha$. For $\alpha \in \mathbb Z$ this holds, since then $N(\alpha) = \alpha^{[K:\mathbb Q]}$; for $\alpha = 2 + i$ it fails at the prime $(2 - i)$. Coykendall and Kettinger's proof of their Theorem 4.2 shows correctly that $\mathcal O_K[1/\alpha]$ is integrally closed and that $1/\alpha$ is integral over $\mathbb Z[1/N(\alpha)]$; what it needs in addition, and what fails here, is that $\mathcal O_K[1/\alpha]$ contain $1/N(\alpha)$.

blocks.title: Conjugation and localisation
blocks.body: Coykendall and Kettinger (Example 5.1, Theorem 5.8) ask when a Galois automorphism $\sigma$ preserves an overring of $\mathcal O_K$. Let $D = \mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$, $\sigma$ complex conjugation and $\alpha = 1 + \sqrt{-5}$. blocks.title: Local rings at points: multiplicities and computation
blocks.body:
In computational algebraic geometry localisation appears in its most literal form. For a point $o$ of affine space $\mathbb A^n_k$, Boehm, Decker and Schreyer work with the local ring
$$\mathcal O_o = k[x_1, \dots, x_n]_{\mathfrak m_o} = \{g/h : h(o) \ne 0\},$$
where $\mathfrak m_o$ is the maximal ideal of polynomials vanishing at $o$; after a translation one may assume $o$ is the origin. Local invariants of curves and surfaces, such as intersection multiplicities and the delta invariant of a singular point, are defined by finite-dimensional quotients of $\mathcal O_o$. The point of localising is that it isolates one point: a quotient $k[x]/I$ supported at finitely many points splits into a product of local pieces, and localising at one of them picks out its piece.

blocks.title: A finite-dimensional quotient is the product of its localisations
blocks.body:
Let $B = k[x_1, \dots, x_n]/I$ be finite-dimensional over $k$. Then $B$ has finitely many maximal ideals $\mathfrak m_1, \dots, \mathfrak m_r$, each localisation $B_{\mathfrak m_i}$ is finite-dimensional, and
$$B \cong B_{\mathfrak m_1} \times \dots \times B_{\mathfrak m_r}, \qquad \dim_k B = \sum_i \dim_k B_{\mathfrak m_i}.$$

A finite-dimensional algebra is Artinian: descending chains of ideals are chains of subspaces, which stop. Every prime $\mathfrak p$ of $B$ is maximal, because $B/\mathfrak p$ is a finite-dimensional domain, hence a field (multiplication by a nonzero element is an injective linear map, hence surjective). If $\mathfrak m_1, \dots, \mathfrak m_{r}$ are distinct maximal ideals, the Chinese remainder theorem makes $B \to \prod B/\mathfrak m_i$ surjective, so $r \le \dim_k B$; hence there are finitely many. The nilradical $N = \mathfrak m_1 \cap \dots \cap \mathfrak m_r$ is nilpotent (it is a finitely generated ideal of nilpotent elements in a Noetherian ring), say $N^e = 0$. The ideals $\mathfrak m_i^e$ are pairwise comaximal and $\prod_i \mathfrak m_i^e \subseteq N^e = 0$, so by the Chinese remainder theorem $B \cong \prod_i B/\mathfrak m_i^e$. Each factor $B/\mathfrak m_i^e$ is local (its only maximal ideal is $\mathfrak m_i/\mathfrak m_i^e$), and localising the product at $\mathfrak m_i$ kills the other factors (in each of them some element of $\mathfrak m_j \setminus \mathfrak m_i$ is nilpotent, and it becomes a unit) and leaves $B/\mathfrak m_i^e$ unchanged. So $B_{\mathfrak m_i} \cong B/\mathfrak m_i^e$. Compare Gathmann's Example 6.25 and Corollary 6.26, which show more generally that the length of a module of finite length is the sum of the lengths of its localisations at the maximal ideals.

blocks.title: Intersection multiplicity
blocks.body:
Let $f, g \in k[x, y]$ be non-constant square-free polynomials without common factor, defining plane curves $C = V(f)$ and $D = V(g)$. Their intersection multiplicity at the origin $o$ is
$$i(C, D; o) = \dim_k \mathcal O_o/(f, g)\mathcal O_o,$$
and at another point it is defined after translating that point to the origin (possibly after enlarging $k$). This is Definition 3.1 of Boehm-Decker-Schreyer; their Definition 3.3 defines the delta invariant of a curve singularity through the normalisation of the local ring $\mathcal O_o/f\mathcal O_o$, and normalisation commutes with localisation by the theorem on integral closures above.

blocks.title: Two tangential cusps (Boehm-Decker-Schreyer, Example 3.2)
blocks.body: Compute $i(C, D; o)$ for $C = V(y^2 - x^3)$ and $D = V(2y^2 - x^3)$.
blocks.solution: The ideal $(y^2 - x^3, 2y^2 - x^3)$ contains $(2y^2 - x^3) - (y^2 - x^3) = y^2$ and then $x^3$, so it equals $(x^3, y^2)$. This ideal is supported only at the origin: $k[x,y]/(x^3, y^2)$ is already local, with basis $1, x, x^2, y, xy, x^2y$. Localising changes nothing, so $i(C, D; o) = 6$. (The paper computes this both by localising in OSCAR and with a built-in command; the hand computation gives $6$, confirmed in the checks.)

blocks.title: Localising separates intersection points
blocks.body: Let $C = V(y)$ (the $x$-axis) and $D = V(y - x^3 + x^2)$. Find all intersection points and their multiplicities, and compare with $\dim_k k[x,y]/(f, g)$.
blocks.solution:
Modulo $y$, the second equation becomes $x^3 - x^2 = x^2(x - 1)$, so
$$B = k[x,y]/(y,\ y - x^3 + x^2) \cong k[x]/(x^2(x-1)), \qquad \dim_k B = 3 .$$
The maximal ideals of $B$ are $(x)$ and $(x - 1)$: the points $o = (0,0)$ and $a = (1,0)$. At $o$, the factor $x - 1$ is a unit (it equals $-1$ at $o$), so $B_{(x)} \cong k[x]_{(x)}/(x^2) \cong k[x]/(x^2)$, of dimension $2$: the cubic is tangent to the axis at the origin. At $a$, $x^2$ is a unit and $B_{(x-1)} \cong k[x]/(x-1) \cong k$, dimension $1$: a transversal crossing. The total $2 + 1 = 3$ is the dimension of the global quotient, as the product theorem says; and $3 = \deg C \cdot \deg D$, as Bézout's theorem predicts once no intersection points escape to infinity. By the Chinese remainder theorem $B \cong k[x]/(x^2) \times k[x]/(x-1)$, and the two factors are the two localisations.

blocks.caption: The line $y = 0$ and the cubic $y = x^3 - x^2$ meet at the origin, where they are tangent, and at $(1,0)$, where they cross. Localising $k[x,y]/(y, y - x^3 + x^2)$ at each point gives the local multiplicities $2$ and $1$; they add up to the dimension $3$ of the global quotient.

blocks.body: How computer algebra handles local rings. The ring $\mathcal O_o$ is not finitely generated as a $k[x]$-algebra, so it cannot be fed to a Gröbner basis algorithm directly. Two strategies appear in the papers. Boehm, Decker and Schreyer use local monomial orderings, in which $1 > x_i$ for every variable (so that the "leading term" of $1 - x$ is $1$, matching the fact that $1 - x$ is a unit in $\mathcal O_o$), and division with respect to such orderings; this works at points. Sayrafi notes that no suitable monomial orders are known for local rings in general, the exception being localisation at a maximal ideal, where Mora's tangent cone algorithm gives a minimal basis. Sayrafi's Macaulay2 packages, which handle localisations at arbitrary primes, instead compute over the polynomial ring (free resolutions, syzygies) and only at the end localise, pruning the resulting complexes; minimal generators, length and the Hilbert-Samuel function over $R_{\mathfrak p}$ are computed this way. The algorithms are not covered on this page; see Boehm-Decker-Schreyer §2-3 and Sayrafi §1.

1. (Basic) Compute $i(C, D; o)$ for $C = V(y - x^2)$ and $D = V(y)$, and for $C = V(y^2 - x^3)$ and $D = V(y)$.
2. (Basic) Find all points of $V(x^2 + y^2 - 1) \cap V(x - y)$ over $\mathbb R$ and their multiplicities, and check that they add up to $\dim_{\mathbb R} \mathbb R[x,y]/(x^2 + y^2 - 1, x - y)$.
3. (Medium) Compute $\dim_k \mathcal O_o/(x^2 - y^3, x^3 - y^2)\mathcal O_o$ and compare with $\dim_k k[x,y]/(x^2 - y^3, x^3 - y^2)$ over $k = \mathbb C$. Which other points contribute?
4. (Medium) Show that in a local monomial ordering ($1 > x$) the polynomial $1 - x + x^5$ has leading term $1$, and explain why this is consistent with its being a unit of $k[x]_{(x)}$.
5. (Harder) Let $B$ be a finite-dimensional $k$-algebra. Show that $B$ is local if and only if every element of $B$ is a unit or nilpotent.

- [[schemes]]: the structure sheaf of $\operatorname{Spec} A$ is built from the rings $A_f$ on the basic open sets $D(f)$, with stalks $A_{\mathfrak p}$; schemes are locally ringed spaces glued from these.
- [[dedekind-domains]]: Dedekind domains are the Noetherian domains whose localisations at nonzero primes are DVRs; fractional ideals and the class group are treated there.
- [[sheaves]] and [[algebraic-varieties]]: the local ring $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ of a variety at a point is a localisation of its coordinate ring, and the germ picture of the local ring at a point is the stalk of a sheaf.
- [[homological-algebra]]: flatness of $S^{-1}A$, projective and global dimension computed locally, and minimal free resolutions over local rings (built with Nakayama's lemma) are the starting point of the Koszul homology and Auslander-Buchsbaum-Serre papers above.
- [[p-adic-numbers]]: the $p$-adic integers are the completion of the DVR $\mathbb Z_{(p)}$, the "more local" object described in the views on locality.
- [[class-group]] and [[ideals]]: localising a ring of integers kills the classes of the primes that become units.
